passage: In the college computer lab, Rafiq had eleven tabs open for the same laptop question. One review said the battery died by evening. The next said the battery lasted all day. A forum thread called the screen dim, another called it perfect. His friend Pallavi leaned over from the next seat. "You've been reading about this for two weeks." "I know. I keep finding one more thread." He scrolled again, his stomach tight, imagining himself stuck with the wrong one. "What if I pick wrong and regret it?" Pallavi shrugged. "What do you need it for?" Rafiq opened his mouth, closed it, and opened a twelfth tab. His old laptop, hanging again on the desk at home, waited.

qa.q: How many tabs did Rafiq have open?
qa.a: Rafiq had eleven tabs open for the same laptop question.

qa.q: What is Rafiq afraid of as he scrolls with a tight stomach?
qa.a: He is afraid of regret, of picking the wrong laptop and being stuck with it, and each conflicting review makes the doubt bigger.

qa.q: What could Rafiq try instead of opening a twelfth tab?
qa.a: He could write down the two or three things he needs the laptop for and choose among the options that meet them, rather than reading more.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Rafiq's two weeks of reading?
qa.a: Pallavi sees a friend going round in circles and asks what the laptop is for, hoping to bring him back to his own needs.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading endless reviews before a decision, ending more confused and afraid of regret.

passage:
Dear Sarika,
I'm writing because I cannot say this out loud without crying. For a month I have been trying to choose a master's course. I have thirty tabs open. One forum says the fees are not worth it; the next says it changed someone's life. Each thread makes me trust my own list less. I have read so much that I no longer know what I wanted at the start. Last night I got up at three to read one more review, and I felt worse. I think I am afraid that whichever I choose, I will regret the other. Can we talk on Sunday? I need someone to ask me simple questions. Irawati

qa.q: How many tabs does Irawati have open?
qa.a: Irawati has thirty tabs open.

qa.q: What is Irawati afraid of, and what in the letter shows it?
qa.a: Irawati is afraid that whichever course is chosen, the other one will be regretted.

qa.q: What would you suggest Irawati do before Sunday's talk?
qa.a: Irawati could stop reading new reviews and write down what mattered at the start, then bring that list to the talk with Sarika.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Sarika would probably feel concerned and glad to be trusted, and would see that Irawati needs simple questions more than more information.

grounding: Shows a young adult over-researching a decision until more information only adds doubt and fear of regret.

passage: Rehana, twenty, needed a laptop for her design course in Lucknow before term began. On Monday she opened three review sites. By Wednesday she had forty tabs, two comparison spreadsheets and a forum thread where strangers argued about screen colours. Every laptop had someone saying it was terrible. At night she lay awake thinking, what if I pick wrong and regret it for four years? Her friend Sahil found her on Friday, staring at the same two models. "Which one did you like on Monday?" "The grey one." "And now?" "I don't know anymore. I know too much." Sahil closed the laptop lid. "What do you actually need it to do?" She listed three things. The grey one did all three.

qa.q: How many tabs did Rehana have open by Wednesday?
qa.a: She had forty tabs.

qa.q: What was Rehana afraid of as she lay awake?
qa.a: She was afraid of picking wrong and regretting it for four years, which made her keep reading and feel more confused.

qa.q: What helped Rehana finally decide?
qa.a: Sahil's question about what she actually needed brought her back to three requirements, which the grey laptop met.

qa.q: How might Sahil see the forty tabs?
qa.a: Sahil seems to see them as making things worse, and closes the laptop to bring the focus back to her real needs.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading endless reviews and becoming more confused, with fear of regret feeding the research.

passage:
Sachin: "Dilnaz, you still haven't joined a coaching centre for the entrance exam?"
Dilnaz: "I've been researching. There are six in the city. I've read every review."
Sachin: "And?"
Dilnaz: "One has great results but a rude teacher. One is cheap but crowded. One has good notes but someone said the mock tests are too easy. Another forum says the opposite."
Sachin: "How long have you been reading?"
Dilnaz: "Three weeks."
Sachin: "Classes started two weeks ago."
Dilnaz: "I know! But what if I pick the wrong one and waste the whole year?"
Sachin: "Pick the two nearest your home. Go to a free demo class at each this week. Decide on Sunday."
Dilnaz: "Just two? And no more reviews?"
Sachin: "No more reviews."

qa.q: How many coaching centres were in the city?
qa.a: There are six in the city.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling after three weeks of research?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt anxious and confused, afraid of picking the wrong one and wasting the whole year.

qa.q: What did Sachin suggest, and why is it better than more reading?
qa.a: Visit two nearby centres for demo classes and decide on Sunday, which replaces endless reviews with real experience and a deadline.

qa.q: How does Sachin see the three weeks of research?
qa.a: Sachin sees it as costly, since classes already started two weeks ago while Dilnaz kept reading.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young adult researching coaching centres for weeks and growing more confused and afraid of regret.

passage: I'm Dhruv, and last year I spent a month choosing a paying-guest room in Bengaluru. I visited five, read every online review, joined two groups where people complained about water supply and landlords. Each new comment made me doubt the room I'd liked. One day I'd want the one near college; the next I'd read about its noisy road and panic. My friend Jomon finally asked, "Are you choosing a room or a life partner?" I laughed, but it stung. The best rooms got taken while I read. In the end I took one of the last left, and it was fine. More reading hadn't made me surer. It had just made me scared.

qa.q: How many rooms did Dhruv visit?
qa.a: Dhruv visited five.

qa.q: How did each new comment make Dhruv feel?
qa.a: Each comment added doubt and panic, making Dhruv more scared rather than more sure.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do differently next time?
qa.a: Set a few must-haves and a deadline, then decide, instead of reading until the best options are gone.

qa.q: How might Jomon see the month of searching?
qa.a: Jomon seems amused and a little exasperated, teasing Dhruv to show how out of proportion the research had become.

grounding: A young adult recalls over-researching a room choice, growing more doubtful and afraid, and losing good options.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Imran, second year, came in about choosing between two electives, Japanese and Urban Photography. Registration closes Monday. He brought a folder of printouts: forum threads, seniors' reviews, a spreadsheet with eleven columns. He said he had read over two hundred comments. "One says the Japanese exam is brutal, the next says it's easy. One senior says photography changed their life, another says it's a waste." He talked fast and kept rubbing his forehead. "What if I pick wrong and regret it for the whole degree?" His friend Chetan had chosen in ten minutes, and that seemed to bother him even more.
What I did next: I put the folder aside and asked him to write, without looking at anything, why he had wanted each elective in the first place. He wrote "I love taking photos" before anything else. I asked him to register by Friday and to come back if it went badly.

qa.q: How many comments did Imran say he had read?
qa.a: Over two hundred comments.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling as he talked about the electives?
qa.a: He was confused and anxious, afraid of regretting a wrong choice for the whole degree; he talked fast and kept rubbing his forehead.

qa.q: Why did putting the folder aside help?
qa.a: It stopped the flood of conflicting opinions and brought back Imran's own first reason, "I love taking photos", which was clearer than any review.

qa.q: What would change if Imran kept reading forums until Monday?
qa.a: He would probably find even more contradicting comments, feel more doubt and dread, and still face the same choice at the deadline.

grounding: Shows a young adult who reads endless reviews before choosing an elective and ends up more confused and afraid of regret.
